case_data.title: Collective Intelligence Project Global Dialogues
case_data.provide-a-brief-description-of-the-proje:
Collective Intelligence Project's Global Dialogues on AI were launched at the 2024 AI Action Summit, and have taken place regularly since, working with a range of sponsors and partners.

In the dialogues, participants take part in an "online collective-dialogue session" of 15 - 60 minutes, hosted on the remesh.ai platform where they respond to structured prompts, submit free text responses, and evaluate statements put forward by other participants. This asynchronous process creates quantitative and qualitative measures of agreement and difference.

The questions include longitudinal indicators, repeated regularly in rounds of the dialogue to track change over time, and research questions to test hypotheses posed by partners for each research round. These may use scenario vignettes or open ended prompts to gather feedback.

Sessions might include framing materials shared by a process moderator, and the remesh platform carries out live analysis to surface statements that appear to have high consensus across different demographics, so these get wider discussion. The analysis draws on bridging algorithms. 

By publishing an open dataset of Global Dialogue outcomes, the project aims to inform a wide range of research and policy projects, and my including partner-specific questions in specific dialogue rounds, it works to inform work in particular policy areas, such as [a 2026 partnership with the Windfall Trust "exploring what the world truly needs, expects, hopes for, and fears from the AI economy."](https://windfalltrust.org/global-dialogues-survey)
project-goals: Qualitative: Capture qualitative evidence on public attitudes to AI
Quantitative: Generate statistical evidence on public attitudes to AI

data.title: Nearly half of respondents (47%) say the primary reason to share AI-generated wealth globally is that AI is built on shared human knowledge, and its benefits should therefore be shared. A further 33% frame it as compensation for job displacement .
data.additional-credit-line: Findings: March 2026 (In Partnership with Windfall Trust)
data.name: Nearly half of respondents (47%) say the primary reason to share AI-generated wealth globally is that AI is built on shared human knowledge, and its benefits should therefore be shared. A further 33% frame it as compensation for job displacement .

data.title: AI is already deeply embedded in people's daily lives. Nearly all respondents (98%) encounter AI systems at least weekly, and over half use AI daily in both their personal lives (56%) and at work (54%), with personal adoption slightly outpacing professional use. Yet there is a clear boundary: 57% have never let AI act unsupervised on their behalf, suggesting people are enthusiastic users but cautious delegators.
